rows.title: Monetary Policy
rows.figure: Fed Dec hike ~77% (from ~68% in Asia); ECB Dec ~89% (Nov 4); BoJ Dec ~80%; BoC Dec ~56% (Nov 3, before jobs); BoE 4.00% after Nov 5 hike; RBA 4.85%; RBNZ Dec <50%
rows.read: The strong US jobs report made a December Federal Reserve hike the market's main expectation again, which firms up the dollar's rate support. Most other big central banks still lean toward hiking, but Canada's job losses and weak European spending give their banks reasons to go slower. For now the rate story tilts toward the dollar.

rows.title: Growth
rows.figure: US payrolls +165K (fcst 65K), unemployment 4.1%, revisions +84K; Canada jobs −4.7K, unemployment 6.7%; euro-area retail −0.7% m/m; German output +0.7%; UMich 51.0; Ivey 58.3
rows.read: The US job market is much firmer than it looked, while Canada lost jobs for a second month and euro-area shoppers cut back. That split favours the dollar over the loonie and the euro. A long stock slump could still weigh on spending if it lasts.

rows.title: Inflation
rows.figure: US hourly pay +0.4% m/m, +3.1% y/y; UMich 1-yr expectations 4.3% (from 4.7%); euro-area CPI 4.0% Oct; Brent ~$97.8; US October CPI due Tue Nov 10, 7:30 AM CT
rows.read: Faster US pay growth adds to inflation worries, though households expect prices to rise a little less than before. Oil slipped back below $100, so the energy push has eased this week. Next Tuesday's US inflation figures are the next big check.

rows.title: Risk Sentiment
rows.figure: Nikkei −6%+, Kospi ~−7% (Nov 6, Asia); US chip stocks ~+4%, S&P 500 ~+0.6% midday (Reuters); AUD/USD 0.6857 (−1.1%); NZD/USD 0.5530 (−1.2%)
rows.read: The AI and chip-stock selloff hit Asia hard, then US chip stocks bounced, so the panic eased without reversing. The Aussie and the kiwi still fell hardest, while the yen and the franc held up against them. Fear and higher US yields together left the dollar the day's clear winner.

rows.title: Terms of Trade
rows.figure: Brent ~$97.76 (−0.5%; briefly >$100), WTI ~$90.24; steepest weekly fall since early 2020 (Reuters); Iran offers to reopen Hormuz for sanctions relief
rows.read: Oil briefly topped $100 on new tanker attacks, then slipped back as hopes of more Middle East supply held. Cheaper oil this week eases the bill for importers like Japan and the euro area. It also takes away some support from the Canadian dollar.

rows.title: Positioning
rows.figure: CFTC Oct 27: funds strongly against CAD, against EUR (real money for), against NZD and CHF, for AUD (real money strongly against), strongly for gold; next report released Fri Nov 6, 2:30 PM CT, not yet loaded
rows.read: Hedge funds hold their biggest bets against the Canadian dollar, so Friday's slide in the loonie went their way. They still lean toward the Aussie while real-money investors bet heavily against it, and the Aussie's fall this week hurts the funds' side. Fresh figures came out this afternoon and will show here once processed.

rows.title: Fiscal
rows.figure: Canada 2025–26 deficit C$39.3B; C$50–60B a year ahead; Democrats control House and Senate; France on negative outlook at Fitch and Moody's
rows.read: No new budget news moved currencies on Friday. A Democratic Congress makes President Trump's spending plans harder to pass, a mild drag on the dollar that the jobs report overshadowed. France's debt worries still weigh on the euro.
